inline.s: He unrolls his sitting mat and loosens his robe a little. This is no sitting meditation — he stretches and yawns with his whole body.
Eleven: Wandering with a Cloth Bag
A cloth bag dangling from his shoulder, a staff gripped in his hand — wandering about like this, he is a sight both hateful and absurd.
Twelve: Holding the Ruyi Scepter
His hand grips the ruyi scepter, yet the scepter only burdens the hand; he wears the sangha robe merely to cover his ugliness.
Thirteen: Holding the Beads and Reciting the Buddha's Name
The Buddha recites the Buddha's own name — where can one hide? Seeking the self by means of the self — why should that be impossible?
Fourteen: Snapping a Reed to Cross the River
The sea of suffering has no shore, and the feet find no firm ground; leaning on a single leaf, he reaches the other shore.
The sea of suffering is boundless, and a lotus leaf becomes his boat; trusting his very life to it, he is old and knows no shame.
The aggregates are empty, yet he clings to the body; the mind is empty, yet he grasps at a solid form — so upside down as this, do not say he does not know it.
In his hand a ruyi scepter, beneath his feet a reed leaf; bustling and fretting, when will he ever rest?
He fears the monsters in the sea and treads upon a vajra club; fists clenched and eyes glaring, as though he had met a tiger.
Light streams out in empty space, scriptures lie beneath his feet; he laughs at the faults of others — how could he be called a monk?
Measuring the sea with a shell, seeking spring upon a branch — the truth stands before his face and he does not see it; how could he be named an Arhat?
Pouring out the sea and moving mountains, stretching out a hand and drawing back a foot — such sovereign powers of miracle: who would dare dispute them?
Let him plant his own feet on solid ground and watch where he steps down; steady and sure as he is, no one is craftier than you.
The nature of the divine dragon cannot be touched; but first seize its pearl, and so it dares not resist.
Here in the great ocean he has found the shallows; calling to mind Bodhisattva Guanyin, he is rescued in time.
Bliss he will not accept, so he lets others drag him along; old as he is, he still knows nothing of ease.
Head covered by a patched quilt, so blissful he could die; let others have their miracles — none of them comes close to you.
Verses on the Twelve Arhats Wading and Lifting Their Robes
1. Gathering His Robe to Cross the Water
Wandering on foot he meets a river, and his road has gone wrong; with nowhere to turn aside, he simply has to cross.
2. One Who Can Wade Carries One Who Cannot
The bold one knows no fear, the timid one fears a fall; but since he is willing to shoulder the other, both come off well.
3. The One Who Reached the Shore First Offers His Staff to the One Who Cannot
Nine parts of ten are crossed, only a single step remains; thanks to that staff, he has no small support.
Already on the far shore, he turns back to look at his companion; pulling him up at the very last — how skillful a means.
5. Robes Soaked from the Crossing, a Boy Wrings Them Out
Not knowing the water's depth, he strides in carelessly; soaked through his clothes, he ends up burdening someone else.
6. Reaching the Tree, He Takes Off His Robe and Ties It Up
His clothes are a tangled mess, sunk in mud and water; though he only dragged them across, he must weary himself tying them up.
7. Sitting Barefoot beneath the Tree, He Sneezes and Shakes Off Drowsiness
All his strength is spent, so he sits at ease and dozes; his nostrils turn up toward the sky, and one sneeze wakes him at once.
8. Tired in Spirit and Weary in Body, He Looks Up at the Dozing One
Though his spirit is weary, his two eyes are still open; he watches that drowsy fellow, who is quite muddle-headed.
9. Tying His Skirt
Just as he was wading, he feared the skirt would wrap around him; having taken it off and then put it on again, his effort was all in vain.
10. Leaning on His Staff, He Sits with Legs Spread Wide
Sitting with legs spread wide upon the rock, his spirit is open and expansive; fatigue is forgotten, and he is wholly at ease.
11. Sitting at Leisure, He Scratches an Itch with His Ruyi Scepter
The place where he itches, no one else can know; with the ruyi scepter in hand, he scratches it as he pleases.
12. Sitting Upright on His Staff, He Turns to Watch a Younger Monk with Bundle and Bowl
Now that he has come to the place of rest, why not simply put it all down? But he keeps the other burdened with a bundle — how utterly muddled.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Mending His Robe
Torn and tattered all over, it must be mended anew; to the craft of needle and thread he does not begrudge his toil.

One worn-out robe, a hundred patches and a thousand mendings; stitch by stitch he labors hard. Every stitch must pierce through — if it does not pierce, he will not stop. Yet even when the mending is done, it serves only to cover his head.
The Arhat Reading the Sutras
He has not yet understood himself, yet he burrows into old paper; within the realm of purity he turns up nothing but dregs.

Born unable to read a word, he forces himself to study the sutras; deaf of ear and dim of eye, to whom can he tell what he finds? The Sanskrit leaves have lain for years, bored through by worms; the strokes of the letters are untrue — all of it is a leaking of secrets.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Subdues the Dragon
That creature so full of wrath cannot be seized by force; with wholehearted compassion alone, he fixes his contemplation upon it.
The black dragon lies fast asleep and its pearl is stolen by the master; were it to wake, how could it let the matter rest?
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Tames the Tiger
Its fierce nature is hard to tame, its power and ferocity unmatched; the master gives up his whole body and spends all his spiritual strength.
Claws and fangs are already bared, its savage temper not yet spent; were it not for our master, the town would have been terrified.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Trains the Lion
Claws and fangs of the Dharma cave — who would dare lay a hand on them? Our master's spiritual power treats them as a plaything.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Floats upon the Sea

The sea of karma is boundless, surging without cease; straight across he climbs to the other shore on a single blue lotus leaf. This body is no body, yet it shoulders the khakkhara staff. Empty water joins the sky, and the mark of no-mark is shown. Emptiness is not outside the existent; beyond the water there is no flowing. Who can give one shout and cut off both ends? Trample the vast void, kick over the ocean; the thread snaps at the heel, and the mind has no hindrance.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Who Crosses the River
He crosses the stream of ignorance, yet is still halfway along; his deluded thoughts are not yet cut off — a gourd bobbing on the water.
Cutting off the current and passing over, he could surely transcend; why then must he rely on a single pattra leaf?
The banana tree's trunk is hollow stuff, quick to rot though it is; had he not borrowed another's aid, he would almost have been shamed.
His footing is not yet firm, the clay vessel is not strong; rocking and swaying, he is fortunate to come through whole.
Going on alone would have been the end of it; why turn his head? If he must wait for a companion, he will only grumble and mutter.
A pattra leaf rests in his palm, blue eyes prop up the sky; striding high and walking alone, our master is still a dragon.
Verse in Praise of the Arhat Burning Incense

The old do not rest their minds, the young do not strive; he pokes the fire and burns incense, never letting a single breath go idle. Nothing was ever the matter, yet he seeks out busyness himself — how will he ever arrive in the land of no-birth?
The Dream Wanderings of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Five
Verse in Praise of Master Bodhidharma Crossing the River

He came west ten thousand li — for what matter, truly? When old Emperor Wu first saw him, doubt still lingered in his breast. Not one word struck home, so he swung his sleeve and took his leave. Snapping off a single reed, he meant to stretch it across the great earth; nine years sitting facing the wall, silent and without a trace of interest. He won but one arm of Shenguang, and his whole body was transformed into a mass of light. Meeting thus, no need to ask about the road ahead — a true man has his own ambition to pierce the heavens.

He did not come for nothing; there was a matter in his breast. Meeting no one who could receive it, he swallowed his voice and held his breath. Brushing off his robe, he went his way without a single backward glance; across the surging Yangtze he cut the current and crossed. Snapping a reed in two, five leaves floated in the sky — a mere substitute for walking, how could it be a miracle? His road ahead was undecided, and he knew not where he was bound; who would have guessed that before the Shaoshi cliff he would fall into nine more years of idle fancy?

He came seeking one who would understand, but met without meeting. Not one word struck home, so he withdrew and went his way. Snapping a reed, he crossed the long river, his feet never touching the ground. Had it not been for the Shaoshi cliff, he would have suffered a great loss. Fortunately he found a true-hearted one to cover his shame a little. He has cheated those who came after into calling it the meaning of coming from the West.
Another: Verse on the Half Shadow
In form he resembles a gray hawk; in mind he is like one seizing a hare. It is not that he has no body — he simply will not reveal it all.
Another: Verse on His Return to the West

He came in too great a hurry and returned too swiftly, his spirit worn and his face ashamed. All he left behind was one broken shoe, with skin but no bone. See him go back to face his venerable mother — what words will he bring her in report? Ah, ha ha. Was it unjust or not? He has set his descendants to weeping at the empty sky.

This matter is every person's own portion — why trouble to come specially from the West? He thought only to bring his capital and seek profit; who knew he would instead meet with doubt and suspicion? Returning home, he is desolate with boundless longing; only on reaching home does he regret coming back empty-handed.
Another: Verse on the Embroidered Portrait

Fundamentally he has no face, so the needlework is wasted effort; yet stitched through and through, not a hair is missing. Even so it is only his whole body, and one gets but half of him. On the Liang king's hall, by the Shaoshi cliff — surely there was nothing like this, with all its calculations. People say it is the first patriarch come from the West; I say it is a grandmotherly heart appearing in the world.
Another: Verse in Praise of Master Bodhidharma

One heart and one loyal gut, he came from afar for the great matter. Meeting no one of the true kind, he found little to interest him. Nine years sitting facing the wall, ice withered and snow grown old; without the man who cut off his own arm, this mind would never have been settled. It was only because he himself had hurried at the start that today he knows he came too early.

He came from very far, his heart bore very great bitterness. Meeting no master of the craft, he met with much scorn. Once his Way shone forth, its grace spread ever wider. His life hung by a thread on a single reed, yet he won descendants beyond counting. The whole heaven and the whole earth all take refuge in him — this is our master, the true first patriarch.

A matter lay in his heart, and he could not hold back his laughter. Ten myriad li from the West he came — who was there to understand him? Not one word matched, and so nine years facing the wall. Had it not been for Shenguang, he would nearly have come to ruin. The sea of suffering has no shore, its waves churn up the heavens; think of it and you fall, tread on it and you perish. Five leaves float in the air, one flower unchanged — from this we know our master is still present today.

His spirit covered heaven and earth, his mind embraced the six directions. Ten myriad li to the West he came, expressly for this one matter. It was not that he would not shoulder it; he simply had no taste for groping about. Not one word matched, so he crossed the river — and crossing water, how could his feet stay dry? Nine years facing the wall, cold and joyless, until he tricked Shenguang into dropping an arm. To this day the great earth runs with blood, and boundless family treasure has been cast away. People say it is the direct pointing and single transmission; I say it is the idle man making his living.

Blue-eyed barbarian, blue-eyed barbarian, ten myriad li you came — for what? Not one word matched, so you snapped a reed in haste and turned away your head, shaming me to death. On Songshan's stone chamber the ice and snow have withered; nine years facing the wall, your lips protrude in silence. Neither joy nor care, how lonely is your heart? Suddenly you open both eyes, and both are blurred. Asked who this stander is, a disciple of whom — he means to open his mouth and loses his life. One arm falls, and his heart and gall revive; the dripping blood runs across rivers and lakes. And tell me, who is there who does not have this matter? I ask you, why did you not finish it?

He came expressly for this, and found no one though he sought. Hastily he snapped a reed and withdrew at once. Before the Shaoshi cliff there was no flavor at all; thanks to Shenguang, he breathed out a little of his spirit. He barely left behind one stinking leather shoe, and his descendants complain that it is broken. How much better had he never come at all: the long sky's bright moon without the least film of cloud.

His going was too swift, his coming was too early; few there are who know him, and he only adds to his vexation. Had it not been for the Shaoshi cliff, this mind of his would nearly never have been settled. Though it is called the direct pointing and single transmission, in the end it only circled outside the gate. His descendants down to this day spread it abroad, and the family treasure has been scattered without stint. Hm! The east wind blows open the spring upon the trees; fallen blossoms cover the ground, and no one sweeps them.
Another: Verse in Praise of Master Bodhidharma in the Stone Chamber

In the gray-blue stone chamber he sat nine years facing the wall. It was not that he had no mind; he simply did not know. Utterly bored, with nothing certain to grasp. He waited until Shenguang's snow reached his waist, and out of empty space one word brought ruin. Five leaves bloomed and spring covered the earth; to this day the eyes are filled with thorns.
Another Verse of Praise
Since he came empty-handed, what is in his bundle? Take it for stolen goods and it becomes a smear of poison. Unable to explain himself, he bears the grievance to this day.
Verse in Praise of the Flesh Body of Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch

One yang returns, and warm breath gradually arrives; three yangs are complete, and all things are spring. One yin first comes, and flowing fire congeals within; three yins begin to interact, and grass and trees at once fall bare. The mighty force of creation can still make things wither and bloom; how much more the unborn, steeped and steamed in every thought. Through the existent he enters emptiness, and the four elements all melt; through emptiness he enters the existent, and the existent is then deathless. Existent and empty both forgotten, he is one with vajra. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all the light of tranquil extinction. Therefore our master is king within the Dharma.
Verse in Praise of Master Yongming Yanshou (with preface)

In my youth I read the Essay on Mind and the Formula of Mind Only, and knew at once that the master was a banner of light. Later I followed my late teacher Yungu and heard that the master each day performed one hundred and eight practices of skillful means; I took them for ordinary labors. Secretly admiring them, I put them into practice, and thereby took in every dharma without exception, thinking I had made good use of my mind. When I grew old and came to Jingci Monastery by West Lake, I entered the Hall of the Mirror of the School and bowed to the shadow of the master's stupa, inquiring into his life and deeds. His disciple Dahe brought out the Record of Conduct. I unrolled it and fell silent, losing myself. I sighed and said: This vast, boundless, subtle and wondrous practice of dharma truly cannot be upheld in even one ten-thousandth part without a vajra mind and Samantabhadra's vows. How much less to uncover the school of mind and melt the ocean of doctrine, to reveal the Dharma nature and gather in all beings — without the three wheels of the Dharma realm, how could one reach its threshold? I marveled and sighed at what cannot be conceived, bowed my head, and made this praise:

I bow my head to the master, banner of light, whose pure treasury illumines the whole Dharma realm. Riding the wheel of great vows, he reveals the three karmas, expressly opening the true eye for living beings. He personally transmits the secret seal of buddhas and patriarchs, blending the ocean of doctrine into one mind. He shapes sages and worldlings beyond all measure and enters at once the sea of samādhi of true reality. A hundred thousand wondrous practices reveal mind only; ten thousand virtues return to the one truth. Since the coming of the Three Treasures, in this land only the master could protect the Dharma; therefore Chinese and barbarian alike all look up to him, all entering the embrace of his compassionate mind. Flying, swimming, moving, growing — none is left out; he takes their suffering upon his own body. Were it not for the contemplation of tranquil extinction and equality, how could he see no mark of self or other? How sad that the deluded multitudes in this final age do not know they are all embraced by his vow-power. He hangs up this Mirror of the School to illumine all dharmas; before his eyes, what dharma is not a Buddha deed? This one virtue of releasing living beings alone enters the gate of Vairocana's Dharma realm. When one's own mind first enters the minds of living beings, how can living beings escape the Pure Land? I take lakes and mountains for brush and inkstone, yet cannot write one pore of the master. I vow that all who rejoice and hear or see may together realize our master's power of mind.
Brief Biographies and Verses on the Portraits of the Patriarchs
Verse in Praise of Kang Senghui, the Patriarch Kang

The Dharma-body relic pervades the whole great earth; its light shines everywhere, and there is no place it is not. Then came a man of the highest order, who followed the light and came seeking its manifestation; thus the Brahma monastery was first opened.
Verse in Praise of the Indian Monk Fotucheng

The man of the highest order hides and reveals himself, his conduct beyond reckoning; his whole being is light, and his workings are naturally distinct. He came and went in the emperor's court as one fondles a gull, then lightly took his leave — such was his timely Way.
Verse in Praise of Master Huiyuan of Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu

Vast in aspiration and lofty in heart, he roamed his mind in the Pure Land; he founded Donglin Monastery and made it his first step. The clear sound of the lotus water-clock has carried its cadence down to this day; all who hear it turn their hearts to him without fail.
Verse in Praise of Master Baozhi

The man of the highest order moves in hiding, his traces unknowable. From where did he come? He was the child of an eagle. Wandering through the world, no one could fathom him; having torn apart his own face, what need was there to speak?
Verse in Praise of Mahasattva Fu

The Way does not lie in the Daoist cap, nor Confucianism in the shoe, nor Buddhism in the robe — there is no self and other. If only you can keep from giving rise to discriminating mind, then you yourself are the master of the three teachings.
Verse in Praise of Master Zhang'an

Like echo and shadow he spread the Dharma's transformation, a dragon amid clouds and a tiger amid winds; whoever raises a banner must have his company. The doctrine and contemplation of one house flourished greatly under the master; he entered the ocean of much hearing, its source far and its flow long.
Verse in Praise of Master Fazhi

The one house of Tiantai took Nāgārjuna of old as its distant patriarch; doctrine and contemplation were clear and distinct, and many who touched them awakened. For five hundred years its bonds were not drawn tight, until in truth our master was born and greatly raised its guiding cord.
Verse in Praise of Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra

The abhiṣeka of Vairocana — this is the mind seal; the true command wholly raised, buddhas and demons obey. Dragon spirits run at his bidding, and a hundred monsters vanish in hiding; therefore the wise one attains great sovereignty.
Verse in Praise of Master Xianshou

In the great net of the Dharma realm, sages and worldlings are arrayed; there is one chief cord alone, and only the master could lift it. Drawing in the currents of ten thousand streams, they all return to the sea of nature; the five teachings are gathered as one, unchanged through all ages.
Verse in Praise of National Master Qingliang

Bearing the great seal of wisdom, he encompasses the Dharma realm; entering the gate of total retention, he possesses the four unhindered wisdoms. Nine feet tall of body, a hundred years in the world; teacher to the gates of seven emperors, his deeds beyond conception.
